tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

## Black-box spec: `camelize`, `underscore`, `classify`, `tableize`

Each probe passed one quoted argv word. The executable’s relevant lines, in order, were lines 3–6:

```text
[camelize("test_"+word), underscore("Test"+word),
 classify(word+"_table"), tableize(word+"Class")]
```

### Exact probe outputs

```text
word=""                -> ["test", "test", "Table", "classs"]
word="_"               -> ["test", "test_", "Table", "__classs"]
word="__"              -> ["test", "test__", "Table", "___classs"]

word="apple"           -> ["testApple", "testapple", "AppleTable", "apple_classs"]
word="apple_pie"       -> ["testApplePie", "testapple_pie", "ApplePieTable", "apple_pie_classs"]
word="applePie"        -> ["testApplePie", "testapple_pie", "ApplePieTable", "apple_pie_classs"]
word="ApplePie"        -> ["testApplePie", "test_apple_pie", "ApplePieTable", "apple_pie_classs"]
word="XMLHttpRequest"  -> ["testXMLHttpRequest", "test_x_m_l_http_request", "XMLHttpRequestTable", "x_m_l_http_request_classs"]

word="foo__bar"        -> ["testFooBar", "testfoo__bar", "FooBarTable", "foo__bar_classs"]
word="_Foo"            -> ["testFoo", "test__foo", "FooTable", "__foo_classs"]
word="foo_"            -> ["testFoo", "testfoo_", "FooTable", "foo__classs"]
word="a_1_b"           -> ["testA1B", "testa_1_b", "A1BTable", "a_1_b_classs"]
word="foo_-a"          -> ["testFoo-a", "testfoo_-a", "Foo-aTable", "foo_-a_classs"]

word="foo-bar"         -> ["testFoo-bar", "testfoo-bar", "Foo-barTable", "foo-bar_classs"]
word="Foo-Bar"         -> ["testFoo-Bar", "test_foo-_bar", "Foo-BarTable", "foo-_bar_classs"]
word="foo bar"         -> ["testFoo bar", "testfoo bar", "Foo barTable", "foo bar_classs"]
word=" foo"            -> ["test foo", "test foo", " fooTable", " foo_classs"]
word="foo "            -> ["testFoo ", "testfoo ", "Foo Table", "foo _classs"]
word="foo.bar"         -> ["testFoo.bar", "testfoo.bar", "Foo.barTable", "foo.bar_classs"]

word="apples"          -> ["testApples", "testapples", "ApplesTable", "apples_classs"]
word="person"          -> ["testPerson", "testperson", "PersonTable", "person_classs"]
word="people"          -> ["testPeople", "testpeople", "PeopleTable", "people_classs"]
word="children"        -> ["testChildren", "testchildren", "ChildrenTable", "children_classs"]
word="mouse"           -> ["testMouse", "testmouse", "MouseTable", "mouse_classs"]
word="mice"            -> ["testMice", "testmice", "MiceTable", "mice_classs"]
word="sheep"           -> ["testSheep", "testsheep", "SheepTable", "sheep_classs"]
```

### Inferred rules

#### `underscore`

Observable argument is `"Test" + word`; `tableize` also applies equivalent logic to `word + "Class"`.

For every ASCII uppercase byte `A-Z`:

- Insert `_` before it unless it is byte 0 of the complete input.
- Convert it to ASCII lowercase.
- Every uppercase byte starts its own segment; there is no acronym grouping.
  - `XMLHttpRequest` becomes `x_m_l_http_request`, not `xml_http_request`.
- Preserve existing underscores, including runs.
  - `foo_Bar` → `foo__bar`.
- Preserve digits, spaces, hyphens, and punctuation.
  - Uppercase after any such byte still receives another `_`: `foo-Bar` → `foo-_bar`.

Rust-equivalent core:

```rust
fn underscore(s: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();

    for (i, b) in s.bytes().enumerate() {
        if b.is_ascii_uppercase() {
            if i != 0 {
                out.push('_');
            }
            out.push(b.to_ascii_lowercase() as char);
        } else {
            out.push(b as char);
        }
    }

    out
}
```

For pure ASCII input this matches the probes.

#### `camelize`

Observable argument is always `"test_" + word`.

- Remove every `_`.
- ASCII-uppercase the single byte immediately following an underscore.
- Consecutive underscores simply keep the capitalize-next state active.
- If punctuation, a digit, or a space follows `_`, `to_ascii_uppercase` leaves it unchanged and consumes the capitalize-next opportunity.
  - `foo_-a` → `testFoo-a`, not `testFoo-A`.
- Preserve all other bytes and existing capitalization.
- Spaces, hyphens, and punctuation are not word separators.
- Existing underscores are not retained or collapsed into anything else.
- Because the harness prefix is already lowercase `test`, no distinct first-letter-lowercasing behavior is observable.

Rust-equivalent core for the harness call:

```rust
fn camelize_after_test_prefix(word: &str) -> String {
    let input = format!("test_{word}");
    let mut out = String::new();
    let mut capitalize_next = false;

    for b in input.bytes() {
        if b == b'_' {
            capitalize_next = true;
        } else {
            let b = if capitalize_next {
                b.to_ascii_uppercase()
            } else {
                b
            };
            out.push(b as char);
            capitalize_next = false;
        }
    }

    out
}
```

#### `classify`

Observable argument is `word + "_table"`.

Behavior is equivalent to upper-camelizing that complete literal string:

- Same underscore-removal and underscore-following-byte capitalization as `camelize`.
- Also ASCII-uppercase byte 0.
- If byte 0 is punctuation or whitespace, it remains unchanged and the following lowercase byte is not automatically capitalized.
  - `" foo"` → `" fooTable"`.
  - `-foo` → `-fooTable`.
- Internal and trailing underscore runs are removed.
- Plural-looking and irregular words are not singularized in the observable result:
  - `apples_table` → `ApplesTable`.
  - `children_table` → `ChildrenTable`.
  - `people_table` → `PeopleTable`.

Thus, for this executable, do not implement Rails-style irregular singularization for `classify`; the fixed `_table` suffix prevents the word portion from being rewritten.

#### `tableize`

Observable argument is `word + "Class"`.

Behavior is equivalent to:

1. Apply the byte-wise `underscore` rule above to `word + "Class"`.
2. Append `s` to the resulting terminal `class`.

Therefore every probe ends in `_classs`, unless existing leading punctuation/underscores alter the beginning.

Examples:

- `apple` → `apple_classs`
- `ApplePie` → `apple_pie_classs`
- `XMLHttpRequest` → `x_m_l_http_request_classs`
- `foo_` → `foo__classs`
- `_Foo` → `__foo_classs`
- empty word → `classs`

No irregular pluralization of `word` is observable because the appended `Class` is always the pluralized suffix. A dependency-free implementation can directly use:

```rust
let result = format!("{}s", underscore(&format!("{word}Class")));
```
